{{Short description|Group in arithmetic geometry}}
In [[arithmetic geometry]], the  '''Tate–Shafarevich group'''  {{math|Ш(''A''/''K'')}} of an [[abelian variety]] {{math|''A''}} (or more generally a [[group scheme]]) defined over a [[number field]] {{math|''K''}} consists of the elements of the [[Weil–Châtelet group]] <math> \mathrm{WC}(A/K) = H^1(G_K, A)</math>, where <math>G_K = \mathrm{Gal}(K^{alg}/K)</math> is the [[absolute Galois group]] of {{math|''K''}}, that become trivial in all of the completions of {{math|''K''}} (i.e., the real and complex completions as well as the [[p-adic field|{{math|''p''}}-adic fields]] obtained from {{math|''K''}} by completing with respect to all its Archimedean and non Archimedean [[valuation (algebra)|valuations]] {{math|''v''}}). Thus, in terms of [[Galois cohomology]], {{math|Ш(''A''/''K'')}} can be defined as

:<math>\bigcap_v\mathrm{ker}\left(H^1\left(G_K,A\right)\rightarrow H^1\left(G_{K_v},A_v\right)\right).</math>

This group was introduced by [[Serge Lang]] and [[John Tate (mathematician)|John Tate]]{{sfn|Lang|Tate|1958}} and [[Igor Shafarevich]].{{sfn|Shafarevich|1959}} [[J. W. S. Cassels|Cassels]] introduced the notation {{math|Ш(''A''/''K'')}}, where {{math|Ш}} is the [[Cyrillic]] letter "[[Sha (Cyrillic)|Sha]]",{{sfn|Cassels|1962b}} for Shafarevich, replacing the older notation {{math|TS}} or {{math|TŠ}}.{{sfn|Cassels|1962}}

==Elements of the Tate–Shafarevich group==
Geometrically, the non-trivial elements of the Tate–Shafarevich group can be thought of as the homogeneous spaces of {{math|''A''}} that have {{math|''K<sub>v</sub>''}}-[[rational point]]s for every [[place (mathematics)|place]] {{math|''v''}} of {{math|''K''}}, but no {{math|''K''}}-rational point.  Thus, the group measures the extent to which the [[Hasse principle]] fails to hold for rational equations with coefficients in the field {{math|''K''}}. Carl-Erik Lind gave an example  of such a homogeneous space, by showing that the [[Genus of an algebraic curve|genus]] 1 curve {{math|''x''<sup>4</sup> − 17 {{=}} 2''y''<sup>2</sup>}} has solutions over the reals and over all {{math|''p''}}-adic fields, but has no rational points.{{sfn|Lind|1940}}
[[Ernst S. Selmer]] gave many more examples, such as {{math|3''x''<sup>3</sup> + 4''y''<sup>3</sup> + 5''z''<sup>3</sup> {{=}} 0}}.{{sfn|Selmer|1951}}

The special case of the Tate–Shafarevich group for the finite group scheme consisting of points of some given finite order {{math|''n''}} of an abelian variety is closely related to the [[Selmer group]].

==Tate–Shafarevich conjecture==
The Tate–Shafarevich conjecture states that the Tate–Shafarevich group is finite. [[Karl Rubin]] proved this for some [[elliptic curve]]s of [[Rank of an elliptic curve|rank]] at most 1 with [[complex multiplication]].{{sfn|Rubin|1987}} [[Victor Kolyvagin|Victor A. Kolyvagin]] extended this to modular elliptic curves over the rationals of analytic rank at most 1.{{sfn|Kolyvagin|1988}} (The [[modularity theorem]] later showed that the modularity assumption always holds.)

It is known that the Tate–Shafarevich group is a [[torsion group]],<ref>{{Citation |last=Kolyvagin |first=V. A. |chapter=On the structure of shafarevich-tate groups |date=1991 |title=Algebraic Geometry |series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |volume=1479 |pages=94–121 |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |language=en |doi=10.1007/bfb0086267 |isbn=978-3-540-54456-2|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Poonen |first=Bjorn |date=2024-09-01 |title=THE SELMER GROUP, THE SHAFAREVICH-TATE GROUP, AND THE WEAK MORDELL-WEIL THEOREM |url=https://math.mit.edu/~poonen/f01/weakmw.pdf }}</ref> thus the conjecture is equivalent to stating that the group is [[Finitely generated abelian group|finitely generated]].

==Cassels–Tate pairing==
The Cassels–Tate pairing is a [[bilinear pairing]]  {{math|Ш(''A'') × Ш(''Â'') → '''Q'''/'''Z'''}}, where {{math|''A''}} is an abelian variety and {{math|''Â''}} is its dual. Cassels introduced this for [[elliptic curve]]s, when {{math|''A''}} can be identified with {{math|''Â''}} and the pairing is an alternating form.{{sfn|Cassels|1962}} The kernel of this form is the subgroup of divisible elements, which is trivial if the Tate–Shafarevich conjecture is true. Tate extended the pairing to general abelian varieties, as a variation of [[Tate duality]].{{sfn|Tate|1963}} A choice of polarization on ''A'' gives a map from {{math|''A''}} to {{math|''Â''}}, which induces a bilinear pairing on {{math|Ш(''A'')}} with values in {{math|'''Q'''/'''Z'''}}, but unlike the case of elliptic curves this need not be alternating or even skew symmetric.

For an elliptic curve, Cassels showed that the pairing is alternating, and a consequence is that if the order of {{math|Ш}} is finite then it is a square. For more general abelian varieties it was sometimes incorrectly believed for many years that the order of {{math|Ш}} is a square whenever it is finite; this mistake originated in a paper by [[Peter Swinnerton-Dyer|Swinnerton-Dyer]],{{sfn|Swinnerton-Dyer|1967}} who misquoted one of the results of Tate.{{sfn|Tate|1963}} Poonen and Stoll gave some examples where the order is twice a square, such as the Jacobian of a certain genus 2 curve over the rationals whose Tate–Shafarevich group has order 2,{{sfn|Poonen|Stoll|1999}} and [[William A. Stein|Stein]] gave some examples where the power of an odd prime dividing the order is odd.{{sfn|Stein|2004}} If the abelian variety has a principal polarization then the form on {{math|Ш}} is skew symmetric which implies that the order of {{math|Ш}} is a square or twice a square (if it is finite), and if in addition the principal polarization comes from a rational divisor (as is the case for elliptic curves) then the form is alternating and the order of {{math|Ш}} is a square (if it is finite). On the other hand building on the results just presented Konstantinou showed that for any [[squarefree]] number {{math|''n''}} there is an abelian variety {{math|''A''}} defined over {{math|'''Q'''}} and an integer {{math|''m''}} with {{math|{{abs|Ш}} {{=}} ''n''{{sdot}}''m''<sup>2</sup>}}.{{sfn|Konstantinou|2024}} In particular {{math|Ш}} is finite in Konstantinou's examples and these examples confirm a conjecture of Stein. Thus modulo squares any integer can be the order of {{math|Ш}}.
